attempt 1: note.summary:
The reader commutes 14 km each way and wants an e-bike for it. They weigh about 80 kg, carry a laptop bag, and can spend up to 3,500. The route has one real hill: roughly 800 m long, peaking near 8 percent. Arriving unsweaty matters to them. Two constraints surfaced later and reshaped the comparison. The bike will sit at a work rack, so theft is a worry. They also live on the second floor with no lift, so they will carry it upstairs daily.

They chose a mid-drive over a hub motor, for gearing and less effort on the hill. Their stated priorities are hill climbing, low maintenance, weight for the stairs, and theft protection, with price second. From four candidates they picked the Alder C5. It has a Bosch Performance Line 75 Nm motor, a 500 Wh battery, a 10-speed chain drive and weighs 24 kg, for about 3,200. They took it as the best all-rounder because it supports Bosch's app-based motor lock and is light enough to carry. The trade-off they accepted is chain maintenance, about 200 more over three years than the belt-drive Birch.

The model names appear in quotes and the prices are "around," so they may be illustrative rather than real listings. Running-cost and battery-life figures are rough estimates. The belt-bike total doesn't quite add up from its stated parts.

Still open:
- The test ride itself: hill feel in middle assist, frame fit, carrying it upstairs without the battery, and trying the motor lock.
- Confirming the first free service and the battery warranty terms.
- Buying a Sold Secure Gold or Diamond D-lock plus a front-wheel cable.
- Deciding on insurance, about 100 to 150 a year.
- Budgeting for a likely battery replacement around year three or four, at 600 to 800.
- The Bosch-versus-Bafang question, settled only partly: the case for Bosch rests on the dealer network rather than battery quality.

attempt 2: note.summary:
## Understanding note

The reader wants an e-bike for a daily commute of 14 km each way, about 6,000 km a year. The route has one real hill, around 800 m long at up to 8 percent. They weigh about 80 kg, carry a laptop bag, and have a budget of up to 3,500. Two practical constraints came up later and changed the analysis: they live on the second floor with no lift, so they will carry the bike up stairs daily, and they will leave it at a rack at work, so theft is a real concern. Arriving unsweaty matters to them.

Their stated priorities, in order of weight: hill climbing, low maintenance, carry weight, and theft protection, with price second. They learned the main trade-offs: mid-drive versus hub motor (they accepted mid-drive), battery sizing (400–500 Wh), belt versus chain (the belt saves about 200 over three years but adds weight here), and the Bosch versus Bafang debate. On that last point the real advantage is the dealer network and refinement, not the battery cells.

Decision: they chose the **Alder C5**. It has a Bosch 75 Nm motor, a 500 Wh battery, weighs 24 kg, costs about 3,200, and supports the app motor-lock. The assistant presented it as the best all-rounder. The Birch was the alternative if maintenance mattered most, the Cedar if saving money did. The Dogwood hub bike was set aside early.

Still open: everything on the test-ride checklist. That covers whether the hill is comfortable in mid assist, frame size and fit, whether they can carry it upstairs with the battery out, terms for the first service and battery warranty, and whether the motor-lock works in practice. Lock choice (Gold or Diamond D-lock plus cable) and insurance (100–150 a year) are recommended but not decided. The running-cost totals leave out a possible battery replacement (600–800) near year three or four. The bike names appear in quotes and the prices are approximate, so they may be illustrative. The specs need verifying against real listings.

attempt 2: View 3: build.review: The View answers the question with one order: learn the basics first (motor torque, mid-drive motor, battery capacity and frame style, which together make the "Motor, battery & frame basics" step), then the three shortlisted bikes. Each bike adds its own few steps: Bosch/Shimano plus the app motor lock for the Alder, the internal hub and belt drive for the Birch, Bafang for the Cedar. It reads cleanly. Weak spots: the hub motor and the "mid-drive is the safer bet" reasoning sit only on the path to the decision, not on the bike paths. The frame-style step is thin because the Source never says which frame each bike has.
